newsitem.title: CHINA: China bans conservative magazine blasting Jiang.
newsitem.headline: China bans conservative magazine blasting Jiang.

text.p: China's propaganda tsars have banned an edition of a leftist magazine that launched a veiled attack on new top leader Jiang Zemin just as his sponsor, patriarch Deng Xiaoping, died, sources said on Sunday.

Communist Party propaganda authorities halted distribution of the February issue of China's most conservative magazine, Zhongliu, or Mainstay, which attacked a book seen as pro-Jiang, a Chinese source said.
"They've banned the issue," said the source, who asked not to be identified. The issue is unavailable on the market.
Officials at the magazine said its distribution had been delayed because of the disruption caused by Chinese lunar new years holidays earlier this month.
Political analysts said the article marked a first salvo fired by leftists at Jiang, who was thrust into the position of supreme ruler of China with Deng's death at 92 last Wednesday.
"It's an open challenge to Jiang Zemin," one analyst said.
The veiled attack in the magazine, mouthpiece of hardliners in the ruling Communist Party, came in an issue published as pragmatic reformer Deng lay on his deathbed.

Deng hand-picked Jiang as his heir in 1989 after the army brutally crushed student-led demonstrations for democracy in Beijing and he sacked the incumbent party chief, Zhao Ziyang, for sympathising with the protesters.
While the power transfer so far has been smooth, analysts say upheavals are possible -- especially with Jiang's post as Communist Party chief up for review at the 15th Party Congress later this year.
China's political heavyweights struggle for power behind the scenes in battles that traditionally become known only when they erupt in the state media.

The magazine attacked the book for omitting to support the cardinal principles laid down by Deng as the basis of communist rule such as the leadership of the Communist Party and adherence to socialism -- a serious offence in China.
The magazine slammed the book of essays on Jiang's ideology for suggesting China's authorities should tolerate or shelter hostile foreign ideological forces instead of locking them out.
"If... we 'tolerate' or 'shelter' hostile ideology trying to overthrow us, it will inevitably lead to the destruction of our socialist ideology and culture," the magazine warned.
The language used by the magazine was reminiscent of the chaotic 1966-76 Cultural Revolution that Mao Zedong used to purge his opponents, analysts said.

The magazine is believed to be close to retired conservative ideologue Deng Liqun, a former speechwriter for Deng Xiaoping until their relations soured due to his opposition to reform. Deng Liqun was sidelined by Jiang.
In a sign of Deng Liqun's disfavour, the retired conservative ideologue was excluded from the 459-member Funeral Committee formed for Deng at the request of his family.
An editor of the magazine declined to comment on whether the article was an attack on Jiang.
